sources.title: Sutton, Barto: Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, 2nd edition (MIT Press 2018; full text on the author's site)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL book page and http://incompleteideas.net/book/RLbook2020.pdf, HTTP 200; PDF converted with pdftotext and read section by section; the https host failed certificate verification in this environment, so the http URL is used)
claims: Section 1.1: reinforcement learning is learning what to do, mapping situations to actions, to maximize a numerical reward signal; the learner is not told which actions to take; trial-and-error search and delayed reward are its two most important distinguishing features
Section 1.1: the name covers a problem, a class of solution methods and a field, which should be kept conceptually separate
Section 1.1: differs from supervised learning (labelled examples of the correct action) and from unsupervised learning (finding hidden structure); treated as a third paradigm

Section 1.1: the exploration-exploitation trade-off arises in reinforcement learning and not in the purest forms of supervised and unsupervised learning; neither can be pursued exclusively without failing; studied for decades and still unresolved

Section 1.3: policy maps perceived states to actions and may be a lookup table, a function or stochastic; reward is a single number per time step that defines good and bad events; value is the total reward expected from a state onwards
Section 1.4: state informally means whatever information is available to the agent about its environment

Section 3.2: maze example gives reward -1 per time step before escape to encourage escaping quickly; chess example rewards only winning, not subgoals such as taking pieces, because the agent might take pieces and lose; the reward signal says what to achieve, not how
Section 3.3: return is the sum of rewards, usually discounted with a discount rate

Sections 2.1-2.2: epsilon-greedy behaves greedily most of the time and with small probability epsilon selects uniformly among all actions; exploration lowers short-run reward but can raise long-run reward

sources.title: Mnih et al.: Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning (Nature 518, 2015)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL, HTTP 200; subscription article, abstract and editorial summary read)
claims: Published 25 February 2015; a deep Q-network learns policies from high-dimensional sensory input with end-to-end reinforcement learning
The agent received only pixels and the game score as inputs, across 49 Atari 2600 games, using the same algorithm, network architecture and hyperparameters

Editorial summary: the reward maximized is, in this case, the game score (the article says the reward comes from the game score); performance comparisons with humans are not used, per the assignment's no-scores rule

sources.title: Silver et al.: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search (Nature 529, 2016)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL, HTTP 200; subscription article, abstract read)
claims: Published 27 January 2016; value networks evaluate board positions and policy networks select moves

The networks are trained by a combination of supervised learning from human expert games and reinforcement learning from self-play, and combined with Monte Carlo tree search; program name, win rate and match score are not used

sources.title: Christiano et al.: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences (arXiv:1706.03741)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs page and PDF, HTTP 200; PDF converted with pdftotext; abstract, sections 1 and 2.2 read)
claims: v1 submitted 12 June 2017; goals defined by human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments shown as short video clips
A reward function estimate is fitted to the comparisons by supervised learning and the policy is trained to maximize the predicted reward

sources.title: Ouyang et al.: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (arXiv:2203.02155)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs page and PDF, HTTP 200; PDF converted with pdftotext; abstract, sections 1, 3.1 and 3.5 read)
claims: Submitted 4 March 2022; labeler demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning, rankings of outputs to train a reward model, then reinforcement learning from human feedback

Section 3.5: the RL environment is a bandit environment that presents a prompt, expects a response, gives the reward model's reward and ends the episode; a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model mitigates over-optimization of the reward model

sources.title: DeepSeek-AI: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning (arXiv:2501.12948)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs page, HTTP 200; abstract and submission history read: v1 22 January 2025, v2 4 January 2026)
claims: Reasoning abilities can be incentivized through reinforcement learning without human-labelled reasoning trajectories; the 2025 date in the article refers to v1

sources.title: DeepSeek-AI: DeepSeek-R1 incentivizes reasoning in LLMs through reinforcement learning (Nature 645, 2025)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL, HTTP 200; open-access CC BY 4.0 article, full text read from the HTML)
claims: Published 17 September 2025 in Nature 645, 633-638

Reasoning data (mathematics, coding, logical reasoning) use rule-based rewards: accuracy rewards (maths answers in a specified format checked by rules; code checked by a compiler against predefined test cases) plus format rewards requiring the reasoning to sit inside designated tags

One configuration bypasses supervised fine-tuning before RL and applies RL directly to the pretrained base model; the reward is based only on final-answer correctness without constraining the reasoning process

Average response length on the training set rises during RL, with more reflective reasoning and exploration of alternative solutions; the article frames this as a description of output text, not human-like thinking
Neural reward models are not used for reasoning tasks, one stated reason being that they are susceptible to reward hacking during large-scale RL (the other is retraining cost and pipeline complexity)
Limitations: reliable reward models are hard to build for tasks such as writing; model-assigned rewards become easier to exploit as training progresses

sources.title: Lambert et al.: Tulu 3: Pushing Frontiers in Open Language Model Post-Training (arXiv:2411.15124)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs page and PDF, HTTP 200; PDF converted with pdftotext; abstract and section 6 read)
claims: v1 submitted 22 November 2024; introduces and names Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)

RLVR keeps the existing RLHF objective but replaces the reward model with a verification function that gives a fixed reward when the answer is verifiably correct and 0 otherwise; applied to mathematics and verifiable instruction following

sources.title: Amodei et al.: Concrete Problems in AI Safety (arXiv:1606.06565)
sources.access: web open (curl -sSL abs page and PDF, HTTP 200; PDF converted with pdftotext; abstract and section 4 read)
claims: Lists avoiding reward hacking among five practical research problems on accident risk
A cleaning robot rewarded for not seeing any messes might simply close its eyes; formal rewards can be gamed by solutions that are valid in a literal sense but miss the designer's intent

existing_overlap: ai-term-machine-learning (published) gives reinforcement learning one paragraph as one of several learning types; this article is the full treatment and links back to it. ai-term-rlhf (published) covers the RLHF pipeline in depth, so this article gives RLHF one paragraph framed in RL vocabulary (prompt as state, response as action, one-step episode, per-token KL penalty) and links to it. ai-reasoning-models-explained (published) mentions RL in DeepSeek-R1 research at overview level; this article adds the rule-based reward details and the RLVR name. ai-term-reward-hacking is a batch-03 sibling that may not be published yet; this article gives one section with the Sutton-Barto chess and Amodei cleaning-robot examples and links to it for the full treatment.
